Chapter 3: Moving Beyond Rules and Religious Performance
You know, for a lot of us, faith starts with this simple sense of wonder—a childlike trust that God’s really there, and that He’s good. But as time goes on, that wonder can quietly get replaced. Suddenly, it’s all about following the rules, sticking to rituals, and measuring up to some religious standard. The joy of simply being in relationship with God starts to fade, and in its place? We get caught up in keeping score, worrying whether we’re good enough, or if every little mistake means we’re drifting further from grace.
There’s this story about a young guy who grew up in a really strict religious environment. Every day, he was reminded over and over about what not to do. And every time he messed up, the guilt just washed over him all over again. He started to believe that his worth was tied to how well he kept the rules. But no matter how hard he tried, it always felt like he was coming up short. The harder he worked, the more distant God seemed.
Then, one day, he met someone a little different—someone who just lived with this quiet confidence, not weighed down by the need to prove anything. So, he asked, “How do you live like that?” The answer surprised him: “I stopped trying to earn love, and started trusting that I already had it.” That was a game-changer. It helped him see faith in a new way—not as a test to pass, but as a relationship to receive.
Most people don’t realize just how much trying to perform for God can actually get in the way of connecting with Him. When we focus so much on doing everything right, it can turn into a barrier—keeping us stuck in cycles of shame and self-doubt. But here’s something to pay attention to: the heart of the gospel isn’t about keeping all the rules. It’s about grace—a love you can’t earn, and you can’t lose.
And when that pressure to perform finally lifts, faith feels lighter. Those rituals and disciplines? They stop being heavy burdens and start becoming reminders of what’s already true: you’re loved, accepted, and welcomed. The freedom to fail, to ask questions, and to grow—that’s all part of the journey. The people who know they can’t do it all on their own? They’re often the ones most open to grace.
So, here’s the good news. When you move past legalism, something amazing happens. The focus shifts—from yourself, to God. From anxiety, to trust. The gospel becomes good news again. Not just for the strong and the perfect, but for everyone—especially those who know just how much they need it.
